meta.description: A Raspberry Pi listening to open hydrophone archives for whale calls. Live status, the whales, the places, and what the models hear.
lang.name: English
hero.title: wal.funk_891
hero.lede: A Raspberry Pi listens to open ocean recordings from Monterey Bay and the Salish Sea and tries to tell whale calls from the noise.
hero.nameNote: The name: Walfunk is German for “whale radio”. 891 m is the depth of the hydrophone in Monterey Canyon.

dive.label: From the computer to the sea floor
dive.s0.t: Thousands of kilometres from the Pacific, a Raspberry Pi the size of a postcard wakes up and asks for an hour of ocean.
dive.s1.t: It streams the hour from a free public archive in Amazon's cloud, listens, keeps only what it found, and throws the sound away again.
dive.s2.t: The sound came ashore at Moss Landing through MBARI's MARS observatory, a sea-floor cable that brings power down and data up.
dive.s3.t: About 30 km out, on Smooth Ridge beside Monterey Canyon, a hydrophone has listened almost without a break since July 2015. No light reaches it.
dive.s4.t: Somewhere in the dark a blue whale calls at around 43 hertz, lower than most people can hear. Scroll on to hear one, sped up ten times.
dive.profile: Sea floor along a straight line from Moss Landing to the hydrophone, from GMRT sonar data, depth exaggerated. The real cable route differs.
whales.title: Whales at our stations, and what the Pi can really recognise
whales.lede: 18 whale and dolphin species have been reported off Monterey or in the Salish Sea since 2015; they are drawn here to scale. Show every other living species below with one click, hatched until a station records it. Honest status: the Pi cannot yet reliably recognise any species.
whales.scale: To scale by maximum length according to NOAA Fisheries. Person for comparison.
whales.pitch.note: Hatched: roughly what people hear (20 Hz–20 kHz). Many toothed whales call far above it.
whales.monthslabel: Months with song at the Monterey hydrophone
sp.blue.name: Blue whale
sp.fin.name: Fin whale
sp.npright.name: North Pacific right whale
sp.humpback.name: Humpback whale
sp.brydes.name: Bryde's whale
sp.naright.name: North Atlantic right whale
sp.minke.name: Minke whale
sp.orca.name: Killer whale (orca)
sp.person.name: Person
sp.blue.sound: Very low pulses and moans, about 15–40 Hz, below what most people can hear. MBARI tracks its 'B call' at 42–43 Hz.
sp.blue.monterey: Song heard July through February (MBARI, 2015–2021). Calling follows krill-rich upwelling and shifts from night to day in autumn as migration begins.
sp.fin.sound: '20-Hz pulses': short downsweeps from about 40 to 13 Hz, repeated for hours.
sp.humpback.sound: Long, changing songs of tonal and pulsed units; feeding calls around 500 Hz.
sp.humpback.monterey: Song heard August through June, on every recording day in November. Days with song rose from 34% to 76% between 2015 and 2021 (MBARI).
sp.humpback.status: Endangered (Central America population) and Threatened (Mexico population), US ESA
sp.orca.sound: Clicks for echolocation, whistles and pulsed calls. Each Pacific Northwest pod has its own learned set of calls, like a family dialect.
sp.orca.monterey: Recorded at the Monterey hydrophone at times; which population and how often is not verified. Orcasound's hydrophones in the Salish Sea focus on the Southern Residents: 76 whales on 1 July 2026 (J pod 27, K pod 15, L pod 34).
sp.minke.sound: The North Pacific 'boing': a short pulse near 1.3 kHz followed by a 2.5-second tone near 1.4 kHz.
sp.minke.monterey: Presence at the Monterey hydrophone not verified.
sp.minke.status: Not ESA-listed; protected under the Marine Mammal Protection Act
sp.brydes.sound: Pulses and moans, mostly below 60 Hz; in the North Pacific also the metallic 'biotwang'.
sp.brydes.monterey: A warm-water species (about 40°S to 40°N), so Monterey Bay is near the edge of its range. Presence at the hydrophone not verified.
sp.right.sound: A 2-second 'upcall' rising from about 50 to 440 Hz, and loud 'gunshot' sounds.
sp.right.monterey: The North Pacific right whale's eastern population is under 50 animals; it is very rarely seen off California.
known.0: MBARI's hydrophone sits on Smooth Ridge, about 30 km offshore at roughly 900 m depth, and has recorded almost continuously since July 2015.
known.1: MBARI already publishes detectors for blue whale calls, fin whale calls, humpback song and shipping noise, and used them on six years of data (Ryan et al. 2025).
known.2: Google trained the detector partly on recordings from this same hydrophone. Finding something new means looking for what these detectors are not built to count: rare species, odd hours, unusual sounds.
voices.title: Three voices from one November night
voices.lede: 15 November 2020, midnight to 1 am UTC at the MBARI hydrophone. In this hour the model heard humpback song in 432 five-second windows, blue whales in 125 and fin whales in 90. These are its strongest picks: candidates, not yet checked by a person.
voices.speed.note: Blue and fin whales are played ten times faster, which lifts their calls into the range ears and phone speakers can reproduce.
voices.meta.fast: {when} UTC · {dur} s · played {x}× faster · model score {score}
voices.bars: Bars: the model's score per window; dashed line 0.5. Picture: the original sound, not sped up.
voices.footer: Audio: MBARI Pacific Sound, CC BY 4.0. Species labels are the whalu model's, not a person's: these are candidates.
voices.check.Bm: My check: MBARI identifies blue whale B calls by a band near 43 Hz. In this clip that band does not stand out, so the model may be wrong here. Unconfirmed: a case for a human ear.
voices.check.Bp: My check: the loudest energy sits at 12–20 Hz, as expected for fin whale 20-Hz pulses. Still unconfirmed by a person.
voices.check.Mn: My check: tonal song units are visible from about 100 Hz up. Still unconfirmed by a person.

places.lede: The Pi listens to two archives today. Dozens of other hydrophones around the world publish their recordings openly.
places.map.aria: Map of the North-east Pacific coast with the MBARI and Orcasound hydrophones
places.mbari.role: Main archive: continuous since 2015, about 30 km off Monterey Bay.
places.orcalab.role: Source of the labelled orca test clips (27 Sep 2017, J and L pods).

places.orcalab.name: Orcasound Lab
canyon.title: The canyon the microphone listens into
canyon.note: The real seafloor off Monterey from ship sonar surveys, now at about 50 m resolution (GMRT), heights exaggerated three times. Finer structure such as sediment ripples and rubble is assumed and generated in the browser, not measured. From above, deeper water looks darker because it swallows more light. The hydrophone sits at 891 m on Smooth Ridge, just north of the canyon. Drag to turn, pinch or wheel to zoom, also below the surface. On the dive, boulders, sea pens, fish schools, light shafts and glowing jellies are assumed too: plausible for these depths, but not observed at these spots.
canyon.credit: Depth data: GMRT, Ryan et al. 2009, CC BY 4.0
live.title: Listen to the Salish Sea right now
live.note: Orcasound's hydrophones stream around the clock. You hear the sea of a few seconds to a minute ago: waves, boats, crackling shrimp, and with luck orcas. Local time there:

live.credit: Stream: Orcasound, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. The scrolling picture is drawn in your browser from the sound you hear, 0–8 kHz.
world.title: Open ocean microphones around the world
world.note: Every glowing spike is a hydrophone whose recordings can be downloaded without an account; amber ones are the two the Pi listens to now. Coordinates come from each archive's own metadata. Drag to turn the globe, tap a hydrophone or a group below.
world.gaps: No openly streamable archive found for Asia, Africa or South America.
listen.title: Listen to what the Pi listens to
listen.lede: Southern Resident orcas, J and L pods, at the Orcasound Lab hydrophone on 27 September 2017. Press play: amber marks the calls people heard, the bars show what each model thought.
listen.legend.thr: Dashed line: 0.5, where a window counts as a call
listen.audio: Audio: Orcasound, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. High-passed above 150 Hz and loudness-normalised so the calls are audible on phone speakers.

land.title: A landscape of sound
land.note: Time runs from left to right and pitch from front (low) to back (10 kHz). Height shows how much louder a moment is than usual at that pitch, so steady noise stays flat and calls rise as ridges. The glowing wall moves with the audio when you press play above.
results.title: Can a model hear what people hear?
results.lede: Before anything listens to new audio, it has to pass a test on recordings people already labelled: 462 five-second windows, 119 with an orca call. The pass mark, set in advance, is a balanced accuracy of 0.80.
results.speed: Speed on the Pi: {x}× real time.
model.whalu.note: Never scored a window above 0.5; its scores stayed near zero even on labelled calls.
model.perch.note: Trained on 48 other clips from the same day and hydrophone, so this shows Perch separates calls here; how well it carries over to other places is not tested yet.
smap.title: The sound map
smap.note: Every dot is one 5-second window. Perch turns each into 1,536 numbers; this map squeezes them into two dimensions so that windows that sound alike land close together. Nobody told Perch which windows hold calls, yet the calls gather on their own.
smap.summary: {n} windows from 69 one-minute clips, {calls} of them with a call. On average {purity}% of a call's 10 nearest neighbours are also calls; scattered at random it would be {base}%.

words.title: What the terms mean
w.spectrogram.d: A picture of sound: time left to right, pitch bottom to top, loudness as brightness.
w.window.d: A 5-second slice of audio. Models judge one window at a time; windows overlap by half.
w.embedding.d: The 1,536 numbers Perch makes from a window. Windows that sound alike get similar numbers.
w.classifier.d: A small model trained on labelled examples that turns an embedding into one score from 0 to 1.
w.threshold.d: The score at which a window counts as a call. Fixed at 0.5 before testing and never moved to pass a test.
w.ba.d: The average of calls found and quiet windows left alone. 0.5 is guessing, 1.0 is perfect.
w.gate.d: Set before a step runs. A miss stops the work until the owner decides.
w.throttling.d: The Pi slowing itself down above 85 °C to protect the chip.
w.candidate.d: An unusual detection. It only becomes a finding once a person has listened and checked what MBARI and Orcasound already report.

play.title: Can you hear an orca?
play.lede: Play against the two models on real test recordings, then explore deep whale calls with a sound microscope.
game.title: You against the models
game.intro: Ten 5-second windows from the Orcasound test set. Half of all windows hold an orca call marked by people. Decide, then see what Perch and whalu said.
game.question: Is there an orca call in this window?
game.truth.call: People marked an orca call here.
game.final: You {you} of {n} · Perch {perch} of {n} · whalu {whalu} of {n}
game.why: whalu almost never says 'orca' on these recordings, so it is right only when there is no call. Perch, with a small classifier trained on other clips from the same day, gets most of them.
mc.title: Make the deep calls audible
mc.intro: Real MBARI recordings at their original speed. Drag across the picture to zoom into a stretch, then raise the speed until the calls rise above the red line, where human hearing begins.
mc.hint: Drag across the picture to zoom in. At 10× a 20 Hz call is heard as 200 Hz.
mc.hearing: 20 Hz: lower limit of human hearing
mc.audible: at {x}×, everything above {hz} Hz becomes audible
mc.credit: Audio: MBARI Pacific Sound, 15 Nov 2020, CC BY 4.0. Species are the model's picks, not confirmed by a person. The spectrogram is computed in your browser.
nb.title: How each claim was tested
nb.lede: Every step had a pass mark written down before it ran. Here is what happened, failures included.
nb.audit.t: The Pi passes its health check
nb.audit.d: 64-bit system, 220 GB free on a fast SSD, stable 5 V power supply, no throttling at rest.
nb.env.t: The whale model runs on the Pi
nb.env.d: whalu and TensorFlow install as ready-made ARM packages; the model downloads from Kaggle without a login and uses 1.4 GB of memory.
nb.whalu.t: The ready-made whale model hears no orcas
nb.whalu.d: On 462 labelled windows it never scored above 0.5, even centred on calls. No threshold was moved to rescue it.
nb.perch.d: A small classifier on Perch's embeddings, trained once on other clips from the same day, found 109 of 119 calls with 9 false alarms. Caveat stated in advance: same day and hydrophone.
nb.speed.t: Too slow for the whole archive
nb.speed.d: A two-stage design let whalu pick windows for Perch, but in a song-rich November hour whalu flagged 98.5% of them. Combined speed stayed far below the 10× target.
nb.heat.d: Without a fan the chip reaches 85–90 °C under full load and slows itself down. Power and memory are fine.
nb.blue.d: The model's strongest blue whale pick does not show the band near 43 Hz that MBARI uses to recognise blue whales. It stays marked as doubtful until a person has listened.
nb.plan4b.t: Humpbacks: waiting for a human ear
nb.plan4b.d: The last open question for whalu: does it hear humpback song off Monterey? 300 random windows from 2020 wait for the owner's labels, without model scores visible.
areas.note: Coloured areas are loaded live from NOAA. Feeding areas: Biologically Important Areas II (Harrison et al. 2023, Front. Mar. Sci.; West Coast: Calambokidis et al. 2024), June–November for blue and fin, March–November for humpback. Critical habitat: NOAA Fisheries (2006/2021), not the legal definition, which is in the US Code of Federal Regulations. No migration routes are shown, because NOAA's West Coast data has none for these species.
nb.dclde.t: Not on blue and fin whale calls either
nb.dclde.d: Against 240 blue whale D calls and 47 fin whale 40-Hz calls marked by NOAA researchers off Southern California, whalu found none. A check confirmed the timestamps line up. It may simply not know these call types, or the 2 kHz recordings differ too much from what it was trained on.
nb.decide.t: Decision: listen to a sample now, everything later
nb.decide.d: Perch is accurate but too slow for every hour on this Pi. For now it will hear one hour per day since July 2015, with the hour rotating so that day and night are covered evenly. A fan is on its way. In the long run a small model taught by Perch is meant to hear every hour.
atlas.title: Every sound the Pi has heard, on one map
atlas.intro: Each dot is a 5-second window from the sampled MBARI hours. Perch places windows that sound alike close together; the computer then groups them into lettered sound islands without being told what they are. Drag to move, pinch or scroll to zoom, tap an island to hear examples and see when it occurs.
atlas.sum: {hours} hours listened to ({from} to {to}), {windows} windows, {shown} on the map, {k} sound islands. Rebuilt every night.
atlas.empty: The atlas appears once the Pi has listened to enough hours.
atlas.pick: Tap an island on the map.
atlas.windows: windows, {pct}% of those on the map
atlas.ex.note: 15 s each, original speed: the three windows closest to the island's centre. What the island is has not been checked by a person yet.
atlas.clock.note: Rows: months. Columns: hour of day (UTC; Monterey is 7–8 h behind). Brighter means a larger share of that month-and-hour's windows belong to this island. Grey: not sampled yet.
atlas.orca: {n} windows on this island scored ≥ 0.5 on the orca classifier, which was trained on Orcasound, not MBARI: check by ear.
learn.title: Every label makes the next model better
learn.intro: When the owner labels windows, a small classifier on Perch's embeddings is retrained and tested on windows it has not seen. The curve shows how its balanced accuracy grows with the number of labels.
learn.empty: No labels yet. The curve appears with the first labelled windows.
learn.note: {n} labelled windows so far; {sp}: balanced accuracy {ba} on held-out windows. Dashed: the 0.80 pass mark.

galaxy.title: Fly through everything the Pi has heard
galaxy.note: The same windows as the atlas, placed in three dimensions so that similar sounds form glowing clouds. Drag to turn, pinch or scroll to fly closer, tap a star to hear an example from its island.
tl.title: Ten years of ocean in a minute
tl.intro: Every row is a year since 2015, every column a day. Press play: each day the Pi has listened to lights up in the colour of the sound island heard most often that hour, and the bar below adds up which islands dominate.
tl.note: {n} days listened to so far; {skip} days skipped because the archive is missing or silent. The order in which the Pi works through the archive is random, so the picture fills evenly across all years.

layer.currents.note: Currents: real surface currents of {date} from satellite altimetry (NOAA CoastWatch / NESDIS STAR; Sentinel data courtesy of Copernicus; generated using AVISO+ products). Brighter and longer streaks are faster. Fetched by the Pi once a day; this product shows the large-scale flow without the wind-driven part.
layer.sightings.note: Pink dots: {n} of {total} whale and dolphin records from the last 30 days in GBIF.org, loaded by your browser. Records arrive there one to three weeks late, so this is not live tracking. Many come from Happywhale (CC BY-NC 4.0); tap a dot for species and date.
layer.det.note: Red rings: Orcasound hydrophones where listeners or the detector reported whales in the last 48 hours (Orcasound, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0). The ring marks the fixed hydrophone, not the animals' position; machine reports are unreviewed.
layer.det.item: {name}: {n} reports ({human} by people), latest {h} h ago
layer.det.none: No whale reports on Orcasound's hydrophones in the last 48 hours.
layer.acartia.note: Yellow dots: {n} whale sightings of the last days in the Salish Sea, {day} of them from the last 24 hours, the newest {h} h old. Reported by observers through Conserve.io's Whale Alert and others, shared by Acartia (acartia.io, CC BY 4.0). Brighter dots are from the last 24 hours. Observer names and comments are not shown. If you are on the water there, keep your distance and follow the Be Whale Wise guidelines.
canyon.dive.note: Dive in: a camera ride of about {km} km from the canyon head off Moss Landing along the deepest line of the canyon, then up onto Smooth Ridge to the hydrophone. Sunlight fades with depth as it does in the sea; below a few hundred metres only the camera's lamp lights the floor. The floor's colours are an illustration from depth and slope, not photographs.
card.gbif.note: Records reach GBIF one to three weeks after the sighting.
card.acartia.note: Reported by an observer; position as reported. Keep your distance on the water (Be Whale Wise).
card.orcasound.note: The position is the fixed hydrophone, not the animals. Detector reports are unreviewed.
sound.title: Example sounds ({n}) · tap the whale to play them all
sound.none: No freely usable recording of this species yet.
sound.speed: {n}× faster, so you can hear it
sound.noaa: NOAA clips are played directly from
sound.mbari.note: The Monterey clips carry a model's label, not a person's: candidates.
det.blue: whalu found 0 of 240 blue whale calls marked by people. MBARI’s own call index, recomputed by the Pi from one hour a day, follows the season (correlation 0.67) but narrowly failed. A third attempt with Perch also failed (balanced accuracy 0.55, preliminary, Mac mini).
det.fin: whalu found 0 of 47 marked fin whale calls. MBARI’s call index from one hour a day: correlation 0.81, but just below the mark on “song yes or no” (0.79 instead of 0.80). An attempt with Perch also failed (balanced accuracy 0.65, preliminary, Mac mini).
det.humpback: Google’s humpback model, used the way MBARI uses it, now scores every hour the Pi listens to. The verdict against MBARI’s published values comes once 300 days are in (about mid-December).
det.orca: The orca classifier scored 94 % on one Orcasound test day. Off Monterey it is useless: it fires on one window in five. Of 24 orca encounters reported by people it found 23 (96 %), but it also fired in 27 % of quiet times; 10 % was allowed. Failed (preliminary, Mac mini).
det.minke: The Pi has no tested detector for minke whales.
det.brydes: The Pi has no tested detector for Bryde’s whales.
det.npright: The Pi has no tested detector for the North Pacific right whale. It is extremely rare; only a few dozen live in the eastern Pacific.

cic.title: Does the Pi see the singing season the way MBARI does?
cic.lede: The Pi recomputes MBARI's own call index from one hour a day. Orange: MBARI's published daily values 2015–2021. Turquoise: the Pi. Values above 1.01 mean “song present”.
cic.read.days: {n} days: both “song” {both}, both “no song” {none}, only the Pi {onlypi}, only MBARI {onlymbari}. Agreement (balanced accuracy) {ba}. Red: Pi and MBARI disagree.
cic.note: The verdict was fixed in advance at threshold 1.01 on the first 300 days: blue whale 0.80 agreement but peak in September instead of October–December; fin whale 0.79, just below 0.80. Both failed. The slider only shows how sensitive the result is to the threshold; it does not change the verdict. Computed on the Pi.
step.dclde: whalu on labelled blue and fin calls (DCLDE)
step.gate4c: Speed and heat gate without cooler
step.ci: MBARI call index, blue and fin
step.dclde.r: 0/240 blue D calls, 0/47 fin 40-Hz calls, mark 70 %
step.gate4c.r: 75 °C after 1–2 minutes (3 cores, 2 cores, half time); remeasured with the cooler
step.design.r: systemd timers, crash test passed, sampling up to 80 °C (owner exception)
step.ci.r: one hour a day: correlation 0.67 / 0.81, song yes/no 0.80 / 0.79, blue peak in September
step.science.r: humpback (Google model) in the sampler; Perch on DCLDE and orcas on Orcasound running on the Mac mini (preliminary)
nb.gate4c.d: The pre-registered gate requires staying below 75 °C. With 3 cores, 2 cores and half-time computing the limit was reached within 1–2 minutes; the idle Pi already sits near 60 °C. Failed; remeasured once the cooler is fitted.
nb.exception.t: An exception until the cooler arrives
nb.exception.d: The owner decided to sample anyway until the cooler arrives, up to 80 °C instead of 75 °C. The Pi pauses at 78 °C and resumes below 70 °C. The gate still counts as failed.
nb.unattended.d: Sampler, status push and temperature log run as systemd services and restart after a crash. In the crash test the sampler was killed mid-hour: no half-written file, the hour was redone.
nb.ci.t: MBARI's call index from one hour falls just short
nb.ci.d: The Pi recomputed MBARI's published method for blue and fin whales from one hour a day. The year course matches (correlation 0.67 and 0.81), but the blue peak falls in September instead of October–December, and fin whale song yes/no reaches 0.79 instead of 0.80. Both failed.
nb.humpback.d: Google's humpback model now scores every hour the Pi listens to, used the way MBARI uses it (threshold 0.7). It is judged against MBARI's published daily values once 300 days are in.
nb.mac.t: The Mac mini as a lab
nb.mac.d: Model tests run first on a Mac mini with the same package versions. Once the cooler is fitted, the Pi recomputes everything in full, with timing. Until then Mac results are preliminary.

pp.title: What the places look like
pp.moss.d: Home of MBARI; from here the cable runs through Monterey Bay to the hydrophone 891 m down.
pp.canyon.d: A NOAA image from sonar data: one of the largest submarine canyons in the world, cut into the seafloor off Moss Landing. The hydrophone sits on its flank.
pp.limekiln.t: Lime Kiln Point, San Juan Island
pp.limekiln.d: West coast of San Juan Island on Haro Strait, about 5 km south of Orcasound’s “Orcasound Lab” hydrophone. Southern Resident orcas are often seen passing here.
pp.pt.d: At the entrance to Puget Sound; Orcasound’s “Port Townsend” hydrophone hangs off the Marine Science Center.
pp.robinson.d: In the middle of Puget Sound; home of Orcasound’s “Point Robinson” hydrophone (not streaming at the moment).
amb.live.note: You are hearing the {name} hydrophone live from Orcasound (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), a few seconds behind.
sp.gray.name: Gray whale
sp.gray.sound: Low moans (20–200 Hz) and pulsed “knocks”; all calls together span about 40 Hz to 4 kHz. No echolocation.
sp.gray.monterey: Passes Monterey heading south from December to February and back north with calves from March to May. In the Salish Sea 15–20 animals feed around Whidbey Island each spring, near the Bush Point hydrophone.
sp.gray.status: Eastern North Pacific population delisted under the ESA in 1994; the western population is endangered. All protected (MMPA).
sp.risso.name: Risso's dolphin
sp.risso.sound: Echolocation clicks with characteristic peaks at about 22–39 kHz (DOSITS gives up to over 100 kHz); whistles are little studied.
sp.risso.monterey: Off Monterey all year, most often in August and September. Not documented in the Salish Sea.
sp.bottlenose.name: Common bottlenose dolphin
sp.bottlenose.sound: Individual “signature whistles” (about 2–25 kHz), plus clicks around 110–130 kHz, buzzes and pops.
sp.bottlenose.monterey: Resident off California; when they are most common off Monterey is not verified. Not documented in the Salish Sea.
sp.hporpoise.name: Harbour porpoise
sp.hporpoise.sound: Only very high, narrow-band clicks at 110–150 kHz, far above human hearing (and above what the 16 kHz MBARI archive records).
sp.hporpoise.monterey: Off Monterey a separate population in shallow water (0–200 m), so not at the 891 m hydrophone. In the Salish Sea all year, the most often sighted cetacean.
sp.cdolphin.name: Common dolphin
sp.cdolphin.sound: Lots of whistles (about 8–16 kHz) and clicks up to over 100 kHz.
sp.cdolphin.monterey: Common off California all year, peaking in the Monterey Bay sanctuary in August and September. Rare but increasing in the Salish Sea.
sp.nrwd.name: Northern right whale dolphin
sp.nrwd.sound: Clicks and stereotyped series of 6–18 pulses; no whistles were found. Frequency range not verified.
sp.nrwd.monterey: Off California mostly in winter and spring (about November to April). Very rare in the Salish Sea.
sp.bairds.name: Baird's beaked whale
sp.bairds.sound: Echolocation clicks peaking around 25 kHz, plus whistles and pulse series. Exact range not verified.
sp.bairds.monterey: MBARI hears Baird’s and Cuvier’s beaked whales at the hydrophone “much more frequently than anyone expected”. NOAA: on the continental slope in summer and autumn, further offshore in winter. Not documented in the Salish Sea.
sp.dalls.name: Dall's porpoise
sp.dalls.sound: Only very high, narrow-band clicks at 117–160 kHz, inaudible to people.
sp.dalls.monterey: Off California more frequent in winter and spring. In the Salish Sea most numerous in winter, now rare in Puget Sound.
sp.pwsd.name: Pacific white-sided dolphin
sp.pwsd.sound: Two click types with peaks at about 22–37 kHz; whistles are described but not measured.
sp.pwsd.monterey: Off Monterey all year, most often in August and September; MBARI has recorded them at the hydrophone. Uncommon in the Salish Sea, mostly in Juan de Fuca Strait.
sp.sperm.name: Sperm whale
sp.sperm.sound: Loud clicks from under 100 Hz to 30 kHz, most energy at 5–25 kHz; plus “codas” (click patterns) and fast “creaks” while hunting.
sp.sperm.monterey: Heard at the MBARI hydrophone all year over seven years, with a winter peak. Not documented in the Salish Sea.
sp.cuviers.name: Cuvier's beaked whale
sp.cuviers.sound: Frequency-modulated echolocation clicks around 42 kHz (about 31–53 kHz), each only 0.2 ms long. Social sounds not verified.
sp.cuviers.monterey: MBARI hears it often at the hydrophone. According to NOAA its seasons are not known. Not documented in the Salish Sea.
sp.pygmysperm.name: Pygmy sperm whale
sp.pygmysperm.sound: Very high, narrow-band clicks peaking around 125–130 kHz, inaudible to people.
sp.pygmysperm.monterey: Lives offshore in the California Current; seasons unknown. Not documented in the Salish Sea.

hbk.title: Handbook
hbk.lede: How wal.funk_891 works: what it does, what it is built from, where every number comes from, and what it cannot do yet.
hbk.auto: The facts in this handbook (versions, files, tests, sources) are generated anew with every build of the page; the text is kept in English, German and Chinese.
hbk.overview.p1: wal.funk_891 is a Raspberry Pi in a private home that listens to public underwater recordings: the MBARI hydrophone 891 m down in Monterey Canyon, California, and the Orcasound hydrophones in the Salish Sea. It tries to tell whale calls from noise and shows everything it does on this public page.
hbk.overview.p2: Every claim on the page is either a measured number, a cited source, or marked as an assumption. Detectors only count once they have passed a test whose pass mark was written down before it ran.
hbk.overview.p3: The name: Walfunk is German for “whale radio”; 891 m is the depth of the MBARI hydrophone.
hbk.arch.p1: Five parts, connected only by outgoing internet traffic: the Pi opens no port to the outside.
hbk.arch.alt: Diagram: open archives feed the Raspberry Pi, the Pi pushes results to GitHub, GitHub Pages serves the page; a Mac mini tests models first.
hbk.arch.src.d: MBARI Pacific Sound (AWS)|Orcasound (AWS)|NOAA NCEI, GBIF, GMRT
hbk.arch.pi.d: listens one hour per day|Perch, humpback model|timers, health log
hbk.arch.gh.d: status.json every 30 min|code, data, translations|history of every change
hbk.arch.page.d: GitHub Pages, static|runs in your browser|3D, maps, sound
hbk.arch.mac.d: tests models first|same locked versions|Pi repeats all later
hbk.arch.p2: The Pi downloads one hour of audio at a time with range requests, analyses it and throws the audio away; it keeps only numbers (embeddings, scores, temperatures). Every 30 minutes it pushes a small status file to the public repository with a key that can write to that one repository only.
hbk.arch.p3: The page has no server of its own. It is a set of files on GitHub Pages; everything you see is computed in your browser from those files and from public services (maps, sightings, live streams).
hbk.stack.p1: No frameworks and no build tools: plain files that can be read and checked. The tables below are read from the page and the Pi at build time.

hbk.tests.p1: Every step from the project brief ends in a gate with a pass mark fixed before the step ran. Failures stay visible.
hbk.ops.p1: Three services keep the Pi working without anyone watching:
hbk.svc.sampler: starts the sampler 5 minutes after boot and 10 minutes after each run; at most 4 hours per run, resumable
hbk.svc.push: every 30 minutes: export the status and push it to the page
hbk.svc.health: temperature, throttling, load and SSD temperature every minute
hbk.ops.p2: Heat: the Pi has no fan yet. The sampler pauses at 78 °C and resumes below 70 °C (owner exception until the cooler arrives; the project brief’s limit is 75 °C).
hbk.ops.p3: Safety: no inbound ports, no credentials for any data, a deploy key that can write to one repository only. Every result is written to a temporary file and renamed, so a crash never leaves half a result.
hbk.ops.p4: Each change to the page runs a check that all three languages are complete, stamps a new build number into every file, and regenerates the facts in this handbook.
hbk.use.p1: The page is one long scroll in six chapters. The bar at the top shows where you are and jumps to any chapter; each chapter ends with previous and next.
hbk.use.p2: Most views can be opened full screen (icon at the top right), dragged, zoomed and played. The live ocean in the background can be switched off in the top bar; it fades out whenever another sound plays.
hbk.use.p3: Language: top right. Every text exists in English, German and Chinese.
hbk.limits.p1: Today the Pi cannot reliably recognise any whale species. Every detector tested so far either failed or works only at another station.
hbk.limits.p2: Assumed, not measured: the fine structure of the canyon below 50 m, the life shown on the dive, the computer-graphics humpback. These are labelled where they appear.
hbk.limits.p3: Model tests run first on a Mac mini; all of them will be repeated on the Pi once the cooler is fitted, so the project can say it ran on a Raspberry Pi.

pap.title: Listening for whales on a Raspberry Pi: pre-registered tests of open detectors on public hydrophone archives
pap.authors: wal.funk_891 project · working draft, not peer reviewed
pap.status: Draft generated from build {build}. Numbers update automatically with every new result; text last revised 23 Nov 2026.
pap.abs: We ask whether a single-board computer can listen to open hydrophone archives and recognise whale calls reliably enough to be useful. A Raspberry Pi 5 samples the MBARI MARS hydrophone in Monterey Canyon and the Orcasound hydrophones in the Salish Sea and tests detectors against pass marks fixed before each run. Of {total} pre-registered measures so far, {pass} passed, {fail} failed and {pending} are still running. A small classifier on Perch 2.0 embeddings separated labelled orca calls well on one Orcasound day (balanced accuracy {s3p}), while Google’s multispecies whale model did not ({s3w}). Recomputing MBARI’s published call index from one hour per day reproduced the seasonal course of blue and fin whale song (Spearman {cbr} and {cfr}) but narrowly missed the presence and peak-month marks. Without a fan the Pi cannot keep below 75 °C under load; under an owner-approved 80 °C exception it samples at {samp}× real time. We report failures alongside passes and treat every detection as a candidate until a person has listened to it.
pap.intro.p1: Long-term hydrophone archives such as MBARI Pacific Sound (since 2015) and the Orcasound network are freely available, and general-purpose audio models such as Google’s Perch 2.0 turn short sound windows into compact embeddings. Together they suggest that whale monitoring might run on cheap hardware at home.
pap.intro.p2: Whether this works is an empirical question: off-the-shelf models may not transfer to a new hydrophone, low-frequency calls of blue and fin whales may not survive the models’ preprocessing, and a small computer without active cooling may be too slow or too hot.
pap.intro.p3: We therefore ran every step as a test with a pass mark written down beforehand, and we publish all results, including the failures, on a public page and in this draft.
pap.m.station: Station. Raspberry Pi 5 (8 GB RAM, NVMe SSD, passive heatsink), Debian 13, Python 3.13 with a locked environment. Audio is streamed by range request from the public archives, analysed and discarded; only numbers are kept. Status is pushed to a public repository every 30 minutes; the Pi accepts no inbound connections.
pap.m.models: Models. Perch 2.0 (CPU build; 5 s windows at 32 kHz, 1,536-dimensional embeddings) with logistic-regression classifiers trained on human labels; Google’s multispecies whale model (whalu); Google’s humpback song CNN used exactly as described by MBARI (10 kHz, 1 s scores, threshold 0.7); MBARI’s call index for blue and fin whales recomputed from the 2 kHz archive.
pap.m.prereg: Pre-registration. For every test the data, the decision rule and the pass mark were committed to the project repository before the run. Deviations (for example a missing archive day) were recorded before any labels or scores were seen. The main mark for classifiers is balanced accuracy ≥ 0.80; recall marks are ≥ 0.70.
pap.m.tests: Tests. (i) Orca calls in labelled Orcasound windows; (ii) human-labelled blue whale D calls and fin whale 40-Hz calls from DCLDE 2015, used for whalu and for Perch-based classifiers trained on the development split and scored on the evaluation split; (iii) the Pi’s hourly call index against MBARI’s published daily values (Spearman correlation ≥ 0.60, presence agreement ≥ 0.80, peak month October–December); (iv) humpback song against MBARI’s published daily metric; (v) speed, heat and unattended operation of the Pi.
pap.m.compute: Computation. Hardware-independent model tests were first run on a Mac mini with the identical locked package versions; these results are marked as preliminary and will be recomputed on the Pi once active cooling is fitted. Speed and heat are measured on the Pi only.
pap.r.p1: Table 1 lists every pre-registered measure with its data, sample size, result, pass mark and verdict.
pap.tab1: Table 1. All pre-registered measures. Pass marks were fixed before each run; “running” rows are filled in automatically when the test finishes.
pap.r.orca: Orcas. On labelled Orcasound windows the Perch-based classifier reached a balanced accuracy of {s3p}, whalu {s3w}. The orca classifier fired on many windows at MBARI and is not used there; its test against human-reported encounters on Orcasound is listed in Table 1.
pap.r.bluefin: Blue and fin whales. whalu found none of the labelled DCLDE calls. A Perch classifier on the same data (preliminary, Mac mini) reached a balanced accuracy of {s7ab} for blue whale D calls and {s7af} for fin whale 40 Hz calls on the test split, both below the mark of 0.80.
pap.r.ci: MBARI’s call index from one hour per day followed MBARI’s published daily values (Spearman {cbr} for blue, {cfr} for fin whales; Figure 1). Presence agreement was {cbb} and {cfb}; the blue whale peak fell one month early. Both species therefore failed as pre-registered, although the correlations are well above the mark.
pap.fig1.t: Figure 1. Monthly mean call index: MBARI’s published daily values 2015–2021 (orange) and the Pi’s one hour per day (turquoise). The dashed line is MBARI’s presence threshold 1.01.
pap.r.hump: Humpback whales. The humpback CNN now scores every sampled hour; the verdict follows once 300 days in MBARI’s reference period are available.
pap.r.pi: The Pi. A two-stage design reached {sp}× real time against a mark of 10×. Without a fan every setting crossed 75 °C within one to two minutes (best: {heat} °C). Under an owner-approved 80 °C limit the sampler runs at {samp}× real time and passed a crash test.
pap.d.p1: Embeddings from a general audio model carried enough information to separate orca calls from background on the hydrophone they were trained on; whether this transfers across days, sites and call types is the decisive open question.
pap.d.p2: Simple, published, physically motivated indices remain strong baselines: from one hour a day the Pi recovers the seasonal course of blue and fin whale song, and more hours per day would likely pass the presence mark.
pap.d.p3: Heat, not memory, limits a fanless Raspberry Pi. Sampling one hour per day is feasible now; listening to every hour will need active cooling and a smaller model distilled from Perch.
pap.l.p1: Training and test windows for the orca classifier come from one day and one hydrophone. DCLDE labels cover D calls and 40-Hz calls, not the B calls and 20-Hz pulses that dominate at MBARI. Several frequency ranges and species facts on the page come from secondary sources and are marked.
pap.l.p2: Some results were computed on a Mac mini and are preliminary until the Pi repeats them. No detection is called a discovery until a person has listened to it and compared it with what MBARI and Orcasound report.
pap.data.p1: Audio: MBARI Pacific Sound (CC BY 4.0), Orcasound (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), NOAA NCEI DCLDE 2015 (public domain). Reference values: Ryan et al. 2025 (CC BY 4.0). Code, test plans, results and this draft: github.com/recurrentanalytics/wal.funk_891.

lab.title: Listen in: is a humpback singing here?
lab.lede: 300 clips of 10 seconds each from the MARS hydrophone at 891 m, drawn at random over six years. You hear them blind: no date, no time, no model verdict. Only once all are labelled is Google’s humpback model measured against them.
lab.how.1: Headphones help a lot. Humpback song sounds like moans, squeaks, whoops and grunts, often in repeating patterns, mostly between 100 Hz and 4 kHz.
lab.how.2: In the picture: song shows as arcs, strokes and sweeps. Ships are steady horizontal lines, noise is a grey carpet.
lab.how.3: Answer with J (yes), N (no) or U (unsure). The next clip follows automatically. Space plays, arrow keys browse.
lab.how.4: Unsure is a good answer. Those clips do not count towards the result.
lab.how.5: Your answers stay in this browser. Download them now and then (below) and send the file when you are done.
lab.all: All clips are labelled. Thank you! Please download the file now.
lab.ref.t: For comparison: this is humpback song
lab.ref.d: Two known recordings. Listen a few times first, and again whenever you are unsure.
lab.data.d: Stored only in this browser. “Download” gives you a file that goes into the project unchanged. “Load” lets you continue on another device.

lab.g.title: You vs the model: is a humpback singing here?

lab.g.say.unsure: Unsure is honest. This answer still counts.

hbk.crowd.p1: Taking part: in the game, visitors hear the same 300 clips as the project owner’s blind test. Only after answering do they see the model score for each second, the owner’s answer and the sum of everyone else’s. Stored are a random id, the listening time and the language. On the GitHub route the sender’s GitHub name is publicly visible on the form; the page says so before sending.
hbk.crowd.p2: Where answers go: as long as no database service is set (data/backend.json), “Send” opens a prefilled GitHub form. A GitHub automation (.github/workflows/crowd-labels.yml) checks every answer, stores it under data/crowd/, recounts (data/crowd_summary.json) and closes the form. With a Supabase project set, answers go straight into a table the page may only write to, no account needed.
